title: Non-Right-Angled Trigonometry

findings.finding: Hold two sides fixed while varying their included angle through acute, right and obtuse cases.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes how the cosine correction changes and how the opposite side increases with the included angle.
findings.checked: The existing four parts change both sides and angles. Independently evaluating the proposed cosine-rule expressions gives 7.21 cm, 10.00 cm, 12.17 cm and 8.84 cm. The method is taught on pages 19–21.

repair.proposal: Append parts e–h under the existing instruction, adding only: 'Predict how the missing side will change before calculating.' (e) Sides 6 cm and 8 cm, included angle 60°; answer 7.21 cm. (f) Sides 6 cm and 8 cm, included angle 90°; answer 10.00 cm. (g) Sides 6 cm and 8 cm, included angle 120°; answer 12.17 cm. (h) Sides 5 cm and 9 cm, included angle 72°; answer 8.84 cm. In each part the unknown is opposite the included angle.

findings.doneWhen: The three fixed-side comparisons are followed by the unpatterned part, with only the single prediction instruction added.

findings.finding: Compare the original triangle with one whose three sides are doubled.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the cosine-rule ratio with preservation of angles under scaling.
findings.checked: Both triangles satisfy the triangle inequality. The largest angle rounds to 106° and the smallest to 35°. Doubling every side multiplies both numerator and denominator of the cosine-rule ratio by four. All required methods are available by topic 5.
findings.assumptions: Scientific calculator available, in degree mode.

repair.proposal: Append: (c) A second triangle has sides 24, 26 and 40. Use cosine rule to find its largest angle to the nearest degree. Answer: 106°. (d) Find its smallest angle to the nearest degree. Answer: 35°. (e) Explain why doubling all three sides leaves the angles found in parts a and b unchanged. Answer: the numerator and denominator in each cosine-rule ratio are both multiplied by 4, leaving the ratio unchanged.

findings.doneWhen: Parts c–e follow the existing question, with one question in each part and the stated answers.

findings.finding: Compare areas with fixed sides and acute or obtuse included angles.
findings.breakdown: The run exposes equal areas for supplementary included angles and shows that area need not increase with the angle.
findings.checked: The supplied practice has no fixed-side run. Using A=24 sin C gives 12.0, 20.8, 20.8, 12.0 and 23.6 cm². Supplementary sine values were taught in nr-p15-teaching-prose.
findings.assumptions: Scientific calculator available, in degree mode.

repair.proposal: Append parts g–k under the existing area instruction. Add only: 'Predict which triangles will have equal areas before calculating.' Each triangle has given sides 6 cm and 8 cm. Include those labels in each part, with included angles: (g) 30°, answer 12.0 cm²; (h) 60°, answer 20.8 cm²; (i) 120°, answer 20.8 cm²; (j) 150°, answer 12.0 cm²; (k) 80°, answer 23.6 cm². Parts g–j vary only the included angle; k is the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.doneWhen: Parts g–k follow part f, with the fixed side labels, one prediction instruction and the stated answers.

findings.finding: The stated area and adjacent sides allow two values of angle ACB, but the task requests a single angle without specifying which configuration is required.
findings.breakdown: The area rule gives sin C = 9.23/27. Both C ≈ 20° and C ≈ 160° produce valid triangles with the stated sides and area. The acute appearance of a diagram explicitly described as not to scale does not resolve the mathematical ambiguity.
findings.checked: Independently rearranged the area rule and checked both supplementary solutions. nr-p15-teaching-prose explicitly introduces these two possibilities; nr-p33-side-a and nr-p38-area provide no condition selecting one here. The intended outcomes exclude ambiguous cases.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator is available. No additional acute-angle condition is supplied beyond the provided stem and diagram description.

repair.proposal: Add to the stem: 'Angle ACB is acute.'

findings.doneWhen: The written givens select the acute solution uniquely.

findings.finding: Use the supplementary interior angle to find the other diagonal.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up compares the diagonals formed by the same adjacent side lengths with supplementary included angles.
findings.checked: The original triangle gives cos ∠BCD=-275/1363. Its supplementary angle therefore gives AC²=47²+29²-550=2500, so AC=50 mm. Cosine rule and supplementary angles are already available.
findings.assumptions: Scientific calculator available; retain the unrounded angle from part b.

repair.proposal: Append: '(c) Find the length of diagonal AC in millimetres, using your unrounded angle from part b.' Answer: 50 mm. The unit instruction applies to this part independently of the stem's angle-rounding instruction.

findings.doneWhen: Part c follows part b and asks for a length in millimetres, with answer 50 mm.

findings.finding: Extend the race-course question by scaling the course while keeping its angles fixed.
findings.breakdown: This connects the sine rule's fixed angle ratios with proportional changes in side lengths and perimeter.
findings.checked: The supplied side lengths and perimeter imply BC = 2 km. Doubling all lengths gives a perimeter of approximately 10.91 km. The sine-rule teaching supplies the required method.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator is available; the second course retains the original course's angles.

repair.proposal: Append to nr-p10-q5: (a) A second triangular course has the same angles, but BC is 4 km. Find its total distance to 2 decimal places. Answer: 10.91 km. (b) Explain why doubling BC doubles both other sides. Answer: each side is BC multiplied by an unchanged ratio of sines.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up explicitly retains the original angles and gives the scaled perimeter as 10.91 km.

findings.finding: Compare areas for supplementary included angles between the same two sides.
findings.breakdown: This connects the supplementary-angle sine relationship with equal triangle areas.
findings.checked: For sides 16 cm and 18 cm, both 30° and 150° give area 144 × 0.5 = 72 cm². The supplementary sine identity is explicitly taught in nr-p15-teaching-prose and the area rule in nr-p32-rule.
findings.assumptions: The follow-up refers to the acute triangle in part a.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts after the existing part b: (c) A second triangle has sides 16 cm and 18 cm with included angle 150°. Calculate its area. Answer: 72 cm². (d) Explain why this triangle and the triangle in part a have the same area. Answer: the side lengths are unchanged and sin150° = sin30° = 0.5.

findings.doneWhen: Parts c and d follow the existing parts and explicitly compare the second triangle with part a.

findings.finding: Rotate both ship bearings together while retaining their distances from the lighthouse.
findings.breakdown: This exposes that ship separation depends on the included angle rather than the absolute bearings.
findings.checked: Both bearing pairs differ by 64°. The cosine rule gives separation √(120² + 180² − 2 × 120 × 180 × cos64°) ≈ 166.92 nautical miles, rounding to 167. The follow-up uses the original question's method and numbers.

repair.proposal: Append: (b) Ship A is now 120 nautical miles from L on a bearing of 162°T, and ship B is 180 nautical miles from L on a bearing of 226°T. Calculate their separation to the nearest nautical mile. Answer: 167 nautical miles. (c) Explain why their separation is unchanged. Answer: the distances from L remain 120 and 180 nautical miles, and the included angle remains 64°.

findings.doneWhen: The numerical follow-up and its separate explanation part follow the original distance calculation.
